title: What We Talk About When We Talk About the Love of Reading (Part II)
author: Timothy Shanahan
summary: In this follow-up post, literacy researcher Timothy Shanahan interrogates the evidence behind the widely repeated claims about why reading matters, distinguishing what is well-supported from what is merely asserted. He argues the decline in pleasure reading is not a recent phenomenon but an 80-year trend common to the US, UK, and Australia, driven less by falling reading ability than by newer media now serving the same psychological needs reading once uniquely met. Reviewing claims that reading builds empathy, critical thinking, memory, and belonging, Shanahan finds solid evidence only for reading's effect on vocabulary and language complexity, notes that empathy benefits are specific to literary fiction and possibly replicable through video narrative, and flags that the 'belonging' claim is contradicted by data showing heavy teen readers report more isolation, not less. He is careful to distinguish his relative unconcern about adult reading decline from his real concern about children, arguing that kids who don't practice reading won't reach needed proficiency, and that school-based efforts like 'drop everything and read' periods have largely failed because they substitute one kind of reading for another rather than building genuine motivation. The piece closes with three practical recommendations: integrating literacy across all school subjects rather than cordoning it off, supporting parent read-alouds since that is the one form of reading that hasn't declined, and helping students understand the actual uses and purposes of reading rather than simply exhorting them to do it.
points: Shanahan separates well-evidenced claims from merely asserted ones: reading's vocabulary/language benefit is solid, but claims about critical thinking, memory, and cognition rest only on correlational evidence that cannot establish causation.
He highlights a counterintuitive finding that heavy teen readers reported being less happy than lighter readers, directly undercutting the popular claim that reading fosters belonging.

The empathy-building claim is narrowed specifically to literary fiction (not popular fiction or nonfiction), and Shanahan notes the same effect has been produced by watching video narratives, weakening reading's presumed uniqueness.

He argues 'drop everything and read' school programs largely fail because they substitute one form of student reading for another rather than building intrinsic motivation, since the reading habit itself is being modeled by adults, not transferred to kids.

His three concrete recommendations, integrating reading across all subjects, supporting parent read-alouds (the one reading practice that hasn't declined), and teaching kids the actual purposes of literacy, reframe the policy question from 'get them to read more' to 'make reading's uses visible.'
quotes: I pointed out that this decline is not just a recent trend, but one that stretches back more than 80 years. I also noted that not only are Americans reading less, but the same is true in the United Kingdom and Australia.

One widely noted study found that this only happened with the reading of literary fiction but not with popular fiction or non-fiction. Examining all the research on this issue suggests caution, and these same benefits have been accomplished by watching video narratives.

The claims about reading's purported positive impacts on critical thinking, memory, and cognition are supported only by correlational evidence. You can't tell if reading fosters those abilities or if those who are gifted in those areas are more likely to be readers.

The unsubstantiated idea that reading accords a sense of belonging seems to contradict actual data, teens who read more were less happy than those who read less, probably because of the isolation from social participation that it often requires.

In the previous blog, I noted the many efforts teachers have made to encourage reading, such as "drop everything and read" times during school days. Such efforts haven't born much fruit. Those periods just swap one kind of reading for another.
We need to make sure that our kids know not just that we want them to read, but why we think this is so important, and then we must make those uses of reading accessible.
